newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan lifts ban on import of gravel from China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan lifts ban on import of gravel from China.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday it was lifting a long-standing ban on gravel imports from rival China, cheering supply-strapped contractors and but angering local gravel producers.
"We have decided to allow unlimited import of mainland gravel due to the shortage problem," said Hsu Wen-lung of the cabinet's Board of Foreign Trade.
The board also would allow imports of 74 other Chinese farm and industrial products after reviewing their impact to local farmers and industries, Hsu said.

Taiwan's Nationalist government, driven off the mainland after losing a civil war to the Chinese communists in 1949, has banned direct links with Beijing, but permits indirect economic activities with the mainland.
Taiwan now permits import of 5,184 Chinese products, although shipments must transit Hong Kong or a third country.
The decision, expected to be officially announced by the economics ministry at the end of June, was hailed by local contractors who face skyrocketing gravel prices.
But local gravel operators protested the increased competition.
Eastern Taiwan's Hualien Gravel Operators Association said lifting restrictions would "seriously affect" its business.
Board official Hsu said that due to the extra costs of transport from China, it was unlikely that mainland gravel could significantly undercut local prices.
To cushion the impact, the board agreed to bar importers from using northern Tamsui port for gravel transport, he said.
Tamsui port, which can handle two million cubic meters of gravel a year, is convenient for transshipping from eastern to northern and southern Taiwan where demand is strongest.
Pacific Construction Co Ltd vice-president Kung Pao-hsiang said mainland imports would help ease shortages.
Since late 1996, contractors have bemoaned short gravel supplies and high prices that reportedly have slowed a number of Taiwan infrastructure projects.
Taiwan consumes 120 million tonnes of gravel a year, 94 percent of which is excavated from river banks, according to the economic ministry's mining department.
Prices have soared more than 120 percent in the past 10 months since Typhoon Herb damaged the banks of most major rivers in central and southern Taiwan.
On March 1, the government banned quarrying along southern Taiwan river banks in a water and soil conservation move, further cutting supply.
A senior mining department official told Reuters that Taiwan's local gravel supplies could last for a year.
The government has encouraged quarrying in eastern Taiwan mountains and is promoting a policy of shipping eastern gravel to other parts of Taiwan, he said.
Local governments and councils have strongly opposed the plan, citing pollution and soil conservation problems.
